definition: Light amplification by stimulated emission of radiation: a source whose light is essentially one wavelength, with its waves in step, in a narrow beam.
A passing photon triggering an excited atom to release a second photon matching it in wavelength, direction and phase.
Light waves lined up in time and space; the reason a laser beam spreads far less than ordinary light.
How fast a beam widens with distance, in milliradians (mrad). At 1 mrad a beam grows 1 cm for every 10 m.
A very fine, evenly spread mist that makes beams visible as smooth cones and sheets.
A thicker, billowing mist that shows swirls inside the beams.
A show seen in mid-air: shapes scanned through haze as beams, fans, cones and tunnels.
A show in which the laser draws logos, text and animation on a surface.
Non-representational moving laser patterns.
A soft, gauze-like moving pattern made by sending the beam through rippled glass or plastic.
Haze or fog visibly swirling inside a flat sheet of laser light.
Visible pulsing when the scanners cannot finish a drawing before the eye lets the start of it fade.
The smallest thing laser software controls: an X position, a Y position, on or off, and usually a color.
A galvanometer scanner: a small motor with a mirror on its shaft. Two of them, X and Y, aim the beam.
Thousands of points per second, the speed rating for scanners.
A mirror or filter that passes one color and reflects others; used to merge red, green and blue lasers into one beam.
The US regulatory term for a laser made or promoted for entertainment, display or art.
US FDA approval needed before show laser equipment above 5 mW of visible output is sold or used.
A video projector in which blue laser diodes light a spinning phosphor wheel and an imaging chip forms the picture; no beam is scanned.
A reflection illusion using a slanted transparent sheet; the method behind stage "holograms".
A recording of the full wavefield of light that replays a true 3D image when lit by a laser.
A scanning laser used to measure distance, as on some cars.
